title: HIS-201 Ch. 1 — 3 Numbers & Dates
subject: HIS-201
topic: Chapter 1: The First Civilizations of North America

cards.term: How long humans have lived in the Americas
cards.def: Native American history reaches back at least 15,000 years to the last Ice Age, when nomadic hunters from Asia first entered the Americas.

cards.term: When Beringia formed a land bridge
cards.def: Between about 25,000 and 15,000 BP, falling sea levels exposed Beringia between Siberia and Alaska, creating a possible migration route into the Americas.

cards.term: When people lived at Monte Verde, Chile
cards.def: The Monte Verde campsite in Chile dates to about 14,600 BP, which is older than the earliest accepted Clovis evidence in North America.

cards.term: When the Buttermilk Creek tools were made
cards.def: Stone tools found beneath Clovis layers at Buttermilk Creek, Texas, date to about 15,500 BP, giving strong evidence that people arrived before the Clovis culture.

cards.term: When the Folsom site was dated
cards.def: Radiocarbon tests dated the Folsom bison kill site in New Mexico to about 10,800 BP, confirming that humans hunted in Ice Age America.

cards.term: When genetic research showed three migrations
cards.def: In 2012 a major whole-genome study reported evidence for three separate migrations from Siberia into the Americas, supporting the multiple-migration theory.

cards.term: When distinctive regional cultures developed
cards.def: Between 10,000 and 2,500 years ago, peoples across the Americas adapted to changing post-Ice Age environments and formed distinctive regional cultures.

cards.term: When the agricultural revolution began in Mesoamerica
cards.def: About 9,000 years ago, Mesoamerican peoples began domesticating plants, starting the agricultural revolution of the Western Hemisphere.

cards.term: When farming spread to the Southwest
cards.def: By 1000 BCE farming had spread northward from Mesoamerica to the Southwest, roughly a thousand years after Southeastern peoples began cultivating gourds and pumpkins.

cards.term: When Southeastern peoples began farming
cards.def: Around 2000 BCE some Southeastern groups began to cultivate gourds and pumpkins, and later maize, adding farming to their hunting and gathering.

cards.term: When Mayan civilization was at its height
cards.def: Between the third and ninth centuries CE, Mayan civilization flourished in about fifty urban centers across the Yucatán and neighboring lands.

cards.term: When ballplayers began scoring through stone rings
cards.def: After about 800 CE, Mesoamerican ballplayers could score by sending a heavy rubber ball through a stone ring set high on the court wall.

cards.term: When the Mayan political order collapsed
cards.def: By about 900 CE the Mayan political order had collapsed, though scholars still debate whether war, ecology, or resource strain caused the collapse.

cards.term: How large Teotihuacán was at its height
cards.def: Around 650 CE, Teotihuacán covered roughly fifteen square miles and housed nearly 200,000 people, making the city one of the largest in the world.

cards.term: When the Adena and Hopewell built burial mounds
cards.def: About 2,000 years ago, Adena and Hopewell communities built burial mounds in the Ohio and Mississippi valleys and filled them with imported prestige goods.

cards.term: When Poverty Point's earthworks were built
cards.def: Around 1000 BCE, the builders of Poverty Point in Louisiana raised enormous earthworks, one of the earliest mound centers in eastern North America.

cards.term: When the Anasazi population peaked
cards.def: Between about 900 and 1100 CE, the Anasazi population reached its peak of about 30,000 people spread across a vast area of the Southwest.

cards.term: When Cahokia reached its height
cards.def: By the twelfth century CE, Cahokia had become the leading city-building and trading center of eastern North America.

cards.term: How many people lived at Cahokia
cards.def: At its height, Cahokia may have held as many as 30,000 people, making Cahokia one of the largest cities in North America before European contact.

cards.term: When the Aztecs arrived in central Mexico
cards.def: In the mid-thirteenth century, the Aztecs migrated south from northern Mesoamerica and settled in the Valley of Mexico in central Mexico.

cards.term: When the Aztec empire peaked
cards.def: By the late fifteenth century, the Aztecs ruled a large tribute empire centered on their island capital of Tenochtitlán.

cards.term: How many people lived in Tenochtitlán
cards.def: By the late fifteenth century, Tenochtitlán may have housed about a quarter of a million people, making the Aztec capital a major world city.

cards.term: When many American cultures declined
cards.def: During the three to four hundred years before Europeans arrived, many sophisticated American cultures declined sharply or disappeared for reasons that remain a mystery.

cards.term: When lasting European contact began
cards.def: In 1492 Christopher Columbus reached the Caribbean, beginning lasting contact that would devastate Native peoples through disease and conquest.

cards.term: How many people lived in North America and the Caribbean by 1492
cards.def: Somewhere between 57 and 112 million people lived in over 350 different societies in North America and the Caribbean when Europeans arrived.

cards.term: What share of the world's crops came from the Americas
cards.def: Plants domesticated by Native Americans, including corn, squash, potatoes, and beans, today account for three-fifths of the world's crops.

cards.term: How many large mammals humans domesticated worldwide
cards.def: Of 148 large mammal species worldwide, humans domesticated only fourteen before the twentieth century, so few wild animals were suitable for herding.

cards.term: How Eurasia's domestic animals compared with the Americas'
cards.def: Eurasia had thirteen of the world's fourteen domesticated large mammals, while the Americas had only one, the llama and its relative the alpaca.

cards.term: When Mesoamericans domesticated squash
cards.def: Over 10,000 years ago, Mesoamericans domesticated squash, among the earliest crops of the Americas, long before farming became the basis of settled village life.

cards.term: How many large pueblos the Anasazi built in Chaco Canyon
cards.def: During the first eight to nine centuries CE, the Anasazi built nine large pueblos, multistory stone apartment towns, in Chaco Canyon in present-day New Mexico.
